title: Switch Interfaces
summary: Configuring speed, duplex, and descriptions on switch interfaces, understanding autonegotiation, interface status, and error counters.

sections.title: Switches vs routers: the port count

content.body:
The obvious difference between a switch and a router is the **number of interfaces**. A router (e.g. a Cisco ASR 1000-X) might have a handful of SFP fiber ports plus a console port. A switch (e.g. a Catalyst 9200) has dozens of RJ45 ports — 48 is common — plus a few SFP uplink ports.

That's because **switches connect end hosts**. A switch may have 48 PCs attached, then link to a router through an SFP fiber port. This lesson covers configuring the Layer 1 characteristics of switch interfaces: **speed** and **duplex**.

In `show ip interface brief`, switch interfaces behave differently from router interfaces:

- **Router interfaces** have `shutdown` applied by default → **administratively down/down**.
- **Switch interfaces** do **not** have `shutdown` applied → they are **up/up** when connected to another device, or **down/down** when nothing is plugged in.

`down/down` is *not* the same as `administratively down/down`. `down/down` just means nothing is connected; `administratively down` means the `shutdown` command was used.

A Layer 2 switchport does not need an IP address — that's why its IP-Address column stays `unassigned`.

`show interfaces status` gives a compact per-port summary:

- **Port** — the interface name.
- **Name** — the interface description.
- **Status** — `connected` (a device is attached) or `notconnect` (nothing attached); `disabled` after `shutdown`.
- **VLAN** — the access VLAN (default 1; `trunk` for the link to another switch).
- **Duplex** — `a-full` means full duplex was **auto**-negotiated; `full` means manually configured.
- **Speed** — `a-100` means 100 Mbps auto-negotiated; `100` means manually set.
- **Type** — the port type, e.g. `10/100BASE-TX` for RJ45 copper.

- **Half duplex** — a device **cannot** send and receive at the same time; it must wait if it is receiving.
- **Full duplex** — a device **can** send and receive simultaneously.

Full duplex is preferred; with switches, essentially every modern link runs full duplex. Half duplex mattered in the era of **hubs**, which are simple Layer 1 repeaters: every frame a hub receives is flooded out all other ports.

Devices attached to a hub share one **collision domain** — if two send at once, the frames collide and neither arrives intact. Ethernet's answer is **CSMA/CD** (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection): devices listen before sending, and if a collision still occurs they send a jamming signal, then each waits a random time before retrying.

Switches separate each port into its own collision domain, so collisions become rare and are usually a sign of misconfiguration (like a duplex mismatch).

Speed and duplex are `auto` by default, but you can set them manually:

```
SW1(config)# interface f0/1
SW1(config-if)# speed 100
SW1(config-if)# duplex full
SW1(config-if)# description ## to R1
```

- `speed` — `10`, `100`, `1000`, or `auto`.
- `duplex` — `auto`, `full`, or `half`.
- `description` — an optional label to identify the interface's purpose.

After manual configuration, `show interfaces status` shows `full` and `100` (no leading `a-`), because the values are no longer auto-negotiated.

To configure many ports at once, use **`interface range`**:

```
SW1(config)# interface range f0/5-12
SW1(config-if-range)# shutdown
```

Ranges don't have to be consecutive: `interface range f0/5-6, f0/9-12` skips 7 and 8.

A good security practice is to `shutdown` unused interfaces.

content.body:
**Autonegotiation** lets two connected devices agree on speed and duplex automatically, using the fastest common settings. Keep it enabled whenever possible.

If one side has autonegotiation disabled (a manual/fixed setting) while the other has it enabled, the enabled side tries to **sense the speed** the neighbor is using. If it can't sense it, it falls back to the slowest supported speed. For **duplex**, it cannot sense the neighbor's setting, so it uses a rule:

- Speed of **10 or 100 Mbps** → **half duplex**.
- Speed of **1000 Mbps or more** → **full duplex**.

This can cause a **duplex mismatch** (one side full, the other half), leading to collisions and poor performance. The fix: use autonegotiation on **all** devices, or configure both sides identically.

Cisco devices count errors per interface; view them with **`show interfaces`** (the counters are near the bottom of the output). The most important:

- **Runts** — frames smaller than the minimum Ethernet frame size (64 bytes).
- **Giants** — frames larger than the maximum frame size (1518 bytes).
- **CRC** — frames that failed the CRC (cyclic redundancy check) performed by the FCS in the frame trailer.
- **Frame** — frames with an incorrect or illegal format.
- **Input errors** — a total that includes the counters above.
- **Output errors** — frames the device tried to send but failed due to an error.

These counters exist on routers too, not just switches.

Classic exam facts: half-duplex devices use **CSMA/CD**; a duplex mismatch causes **collisions** (not improved performance); **runts** are too-small frames, **giants** are too-large frames, **CRC** counts frames failing the FCS check; and **`show interfaces`** (not `show ip interface brief` or `show interfaces status`) is where you find error counters.

questions.question: There is a duplex mismatch between SW1's F0/1 and SW2's F0/1, which are connected. Autonegotiation is disabled. What will be the result?
questions.explanation: The half-duplex side cannot send and receive at the same time, but the full-duplex side is unaware of this and sends data whenever it wants, causing collisions. Performance worsens, and without autonegotiation neither side can sense the other's duplex setting.

options.label: C
options.text: SW1 will sense SW2's duplex setting and adjust

questions.question: What is used on half-duplex interfaces to detect and avoid collisions?
questions.explanation: CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) describes how half-duplex devices listen before sending and how they react when a collision occurs.

questions.question: Which command shows the various counters of errors detected on an interface?
questions.explanation: `show interfaces` displays error counters (runts, giants, CRC, input/output errors) at the bottom of its output. `show ip interface brief` and `show interfaces status` do not; `show interfaces errors` is not a real command.

questions.question: Which of the following are examples of errors that might occur on a network interface?
questions.explanation: Runts (too-small frames), giants (too-large frames), and CRC (frames failing the FCS check) are all real interface errors. Broadcasts are normal traffic, and 'shorts/longs/oversizes' and 'packets/bytes/inputs/outputs' are not error types.

questions.question: SW1 is trying to autonegotiate speed with SW2, but autonegotiation is disabled on SW2, which is fixed at 100 Mbps full duplex. What speed and duplex will SW1 use?
questions.explanation: SW1 can sense SW2's speed (100 Mbps) and match it. It cannot sense duplex, so it applies the rule: 10/100 Mbps → half duplex. The result is 100 Mbps half duplex, causing a duplex mismatch.
